items.body:
## 1. Problem description `GET /api/projects/{projectId}/research-package/preview?defaults=1` computes **five** export profiles (`necessary`, `complete`, `completeWithTrajectory`, `completeWithMemoryGraph`, `completeWithTrajectoryAndMemoryGraph`) in one request. Two of those five walk the session's content-addressed trajectory closure, and that walk reads and `JSON.parse`s every record object in the closure. On a real session in our test instance the closure is **7 740 objects / 3 202 534 318 bytes** (5 442 of them record objects, 3 186 108 662 bytes). The frozen integrity path over exactly that closure takes **56.0–57.2 s** per profile. The five profiles are submitted through `Promise.all` but serialized on a **single global promise queue**, so one dialog open costs at least `2 × 56 s ≈ 112 s` of serial work (derived, see §5.3). The web client does not wait that long: - `apps/web/src/research-package/export-preview-cache.ts:47-49` sets `setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 10_000)` — **without an abort reason**; - `apps/web/src/research-package/ResearchPackageActions.tsx:152-159` catches the rejection and calls `errorText(reason)` (`:49`, `reason instanceof Error ? reason.message : …`), so Chromium's internal string — `signal is aborted without reason` — is rendered verbatim in the export dialog; - because `preview` stays `undefined`, `files` stays `[]`, and `:235` renders `researchPackage.noWorkspaceFiles` ("当前会话没有工作区文件。") for a session that actually has **176 workspace files**, while `:243` disables both export buttons (`disabled={… || !preview}`). So a user opening 导出证据包 on a long-running session sees: two rows stuck at 正在计算大小…, then a browser-internal exception string, then a claim that the session has no workspace files, and an unusable 立即导出 button. Nothing in the server log looks like a failure — the work finishes after the browser left (2 970 × HTTP 200 out of 2 999 `defaults=1` requests in our log dump), which is why this is invisible server-side. The existing `EXPORT_PREVIEW_PENDING` contract does not help here. It is raised when `canWarm` returns false, i.e. **when a run is active** (`services/api/src/research-export-previews.ts:103`, `:119`, `:173`, `:200`), and `services/api/src/http/index.ts:1450-1452` only turns it into `202` if the client sent `Prefer: respond-async` — which the web client does (`apps/web/src/api/plugins.ts:138`) and maps to a **localized** message (`:139-151`). On an *idle but expensive* session there is no pending answer at all: the server just holds the request open for ~1–2 minutes. The gap is "slow", not "busy". ## 2. Minimal reproduction Two halves — (a) shows the server-side cost without any client, (b) shows the user-visible failure. **(a) Server-side cost, read-only, ~1 minute, no model calls** On a Docker instance with a session that has a long `agents/main:/head` history: ```bash # size the closure (read-only; uses the frozen CAS code, no writes) docker exec -i node --input-type=module <<'MJS' const { VersionStore } = await import("/app/packages/cas/dist/index.js"); const { DatabaseSync } = await import("node:sqlite"); const db = new DatabaseSync("/app/data/versioning/refs.sqlite", { readOnly: true }); const row = db.prepare("SELECT target FROM live_refs WHERE name=?") .get("agents/main%3A%2Fhead".replace("%2F", "/")); // adjust to the real ref name db.close(); const store = new VersionStore("/app/data"); const t = performance.now(); const n = await store.validateClosure(JSON.parse(String(row.target))); console.log({ objects: n, seconds: ((performance.now() - t) / 1000).toFixed(1) }); MJS ``` Observed on our instance: `{ objects: 7740, seconds: "57.2" }`, repeat `"56.0"`. To confirm where the time goes (bounded, 25 record objects / 33 MB): | call on the same objects | ms | MB/s | | --- | --- | --- | | `store.read(ref)` — read + sha256 verify | 34 | 968.7 | | `store.readRecord(ref)` — read + verify + JSON parse + dependency extraction | 517 (493 warm) | 64.6 (67.7) | **(b) User-visible failure** 1. Open a session with a long history (ours: 176 workspace files, 226 catalog file rows, 7 740-object closure). 2. 更多会话操作 → 导出证据包. 3. Within 10 s the dialog shows the raw `signal is aborted without reason`, `已选择 0/0 个工作区文件`, `当前会话没有工作区文件。`, and both export buttons stay disabled. ## 3. Expected vs actual | # | Actual today | Expected | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | `AbortError` from the client's own 10 s timer is rendered verbatim (`signal is aborted without reason`) | The dialog recognises its own cancellation (`isAbortError`, which already exists at `apps/web/src/api/client.ts:86-88` and is used by chat paths) and shows localised "still preparing" copy instead of a browser-internal string | | 2 | A failed/absent preview renders as `当前会话没有工作区文件。` while the session has 176 files, and both export buttons are disabled | "unknown yet" and "empty" are different states; an empty list is only claimed when the server actually reported zero files | | 3 | A slow preview holds the HTTP request open for ~56–112 s | The pending contract is not only for a busy runtime: a preview the client cannot get inside its budget should answer `202`/`EXPORT_PREVIEW_PENDING` (or a job handle) and let the client poll | | 4 | One `defaults=1` request computes five profiles, serialized on one global queue, and re-walks the whole trajectory closure once per trajectory profile | The two trajectory profiles should share one closure walk, and sizing should not require deserialising every record | | 5 | Server logs show 2 970 × 200 for this route | A `200` that arrives after the caller aborted is not evidence the user got a preview | ## 4. Source location Line numbers are on SD live main `8a37206be19e4f4d92f52dfa0f08873383a1d50f`, and were re-verified byte-identical on `2d9aa5d344b63b4dca55f92fc3077d0e55d2643d` at submission time (§8). Per-file git blob SHA and size at that revision, so the quoting can be checked without guessing: | File | git blob SHA | bytes | | --- | --- | --- | | `services/api/src/research-export-previews.ts` | `3a2aa07990617f337c4c0d5ee7bdbeec700aaee7` | 13 806 | | `services/api/src/research-snapshots.ts` | `2a0961912d52debfacd03c6ac39dec4ad5b52d5b` | 80 423 | | `services/api/src/http/index.ts` | `e67d07b1d156f185f47216ed2a2959628e595120` | 259 340 | | `services/api/src/artifacts/index.ts` | `776b2154c3ded335b2ca9049d44eb930960ff31f` | 20 155 | | `packages/workspace/src/workspace.ts` | `902c6ca9d14052e6f53ce976f87cbf4464b01353` | 141 829 | | `apps/web/src/research-package/export-preview-cache.ts` | `18dbe2e337b1cbc11f1faca864c8893af4ead40e` | 5 355 | | `apps/web/src/research-package/ResearchPackageActions.tsx` | `c21473542c66a9f205335ece37e516dd28762d39` | 29 207 | | `apps/web/src/api/plugins.ts` | `8341fa5dccbda3c847f71e1f6a5d409b465b2f52` | 11 299 | | `apps/web/src/api/client.ts` | `b25fef29a473fb06696c922147696f7619e1fb74` | 4 403 | The lines that carry the defect: | File | Line | Code | | --- | --- | --- | | `apps/web/src/research-package/export-preview-cache.ts` | 47-49 | `const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 10_000);` (no reason) | | `apps/web/src/research-package/ResearchPackageActions.tsx` | 49 | `errorText = (reason) => reason instanceof Error ? reason.message : …` | | same | 152-162 | `refresh()` → `previewCache.refreshDefaults(...)`, `catch` → `setError(errorText(reason))`, re-armed every `3_000` ms | | same | 112 / 114 / 168 | `files` and `preview` seeded from `previewCache.peekDefaults(...)?.necessary`, `setPreview(undefined)` when no defaults | | same | 235 | `{!files.length ?

{t("researchPackage.noWorkspaceFiles")}

: null}` | | same | 243 | `disabled={busy \|\| scopeGone \|\| !preview}` on both export buttons | | `apps/web/src/api/plugins.ts` | 125-152 | `defaults=1` request, `Prefer: respond-async`, pending → localized `ApiRequestError` | | `services/api/src/research-export-previews.ts` | 139 / 180 | `const work = this.queue.then(async () => { … })` — one global serial queue shared by all projects, sessions and profiles | | same | 188-198 | `defaults()` fans five profiles out through `Promise.all` onto that one queue | | same | 103 / 119 / 173 / 200 | `409 EXPORT_PREVIEW_PENDING`, raised only from `assertCanCalculate` (busy-runtime gate) | | `services/api/src/http/index.ts` | 1432-1436 | preview route: `exportPreviews.watch(...)`, `await exportPreviews.defaults(...)` | | same | 1450-1452 | `202` only when the caller sent `Prefer: respond-async` | | same | 4699 | 3 s `exportPreviews.tick()` | | `services/api/src/research-snapshots.ts` | 481-482 | `includeFullTrajectory === false` empties `entries/untimedEntries/historicalEntries` ⇒ only 2 of 5 profiles pay the closure walk | | same | 597-598 | `const bytes = await versions.read(ref); … addPreviewObject(ref.digest.slice(7), bytes.byteLength, "log")` — per-object byte read (and, for records, full deserialisation via `readRecord`) just to obtain a size | | same | 639 | `await listWorkspaceFiles(store, sessionId, true)` per profile | | `services/api/src/artifacts/index.ts` | 87-89, 108-109 | `if (complete) return readWorkspaceFiles(store, sessionId, true)` bypasses the shared listing cache; scan + `reconcileWorkspaceFiles` per call | | `packages/workspace/src/workspace.ts` | 803, 823 | `MAX_WORKSPACE_SCAN_FILES = 500`; `scanWorkspaceWithStatus` (readdir + stat, no content read) | ## 5. Runtime evidence Instance: Docker test container (`jd-fresh-test-sciencediscovery-1`, `restart: on-failure`, **no CPU or memory limit set** — `NanoCpus=0`, `CpuQuota=0`, `Memory=0`; Docker Desktop VM with 31.35 GiB and 24 visible CPUs), API on 4310 (host 4320), no model calls involved in these measurements. Data read read-only (`file:…?mode=ro`, `docker exec … node --input-type=module < script`, nothing written into the audited data volume by these probes). **5.1 Single-profile cost — RECORDED (direct measurement, frozen code path)** | measurement | value | | --- | --- | | `VersionStore.validateClosure(agents/main:/head)` | **57.223 s**, repeat **56.042 s** (56 MB/s) | | same closure, BFS replica via `readRecord` | 55.539 s | | closure size | 7 740 objects / 3 202 534 318 bytes / 5 442 records (3 186 108 662 record bytes) | | a 191-object / 4.67 MB closure (workspace tree head) | 55 ms | | a 1 006-object / 430.7 MB closure (subagent head) | 6.44 s | | a 1-object closure | 12 ms | **5.2 Where the time goes — RECORDED on a bounded sample, cross-checked against 5.1** | arm | rate | extrapolated over the closure | | --- | --- | --- | | `store.read` (read + sha256) — 60-object size-stratified fit `a=0.208 ms/object, b=0.844 ms/MB` | 968.7 MB/s | ≈ 4.3 s | | `store.readRecord` (+ JSON parse + dependency extraction) — 25 records / 33.4 MB | 64.6 / 67.7 MB/s ⇒ 15.48 ms/MB | ≈ 49.3 s | | **sum 53.6 s vs directly measured 56.0–57.2 s** | — | agrees within **6 %** | The cost is dominated by deserialising ~3.19 GB of record JSON, not by disk IO. This is the same mechanism that exhausted the heap in #1085. **5.3 Five profiles in one request — DERIVED** `defaults()` submits five profiles; two carry the trajectory closure; all five go through one serial queue ⇒ `≥ 2 × 56.0 s ≈ 112 s` of serial server work per dialog open. The client budget is 10 s ⇒ a factor of ~11; raising it to 60 s would still leave the request at ~0.5× of the required time, which is why "just increase the timeout" is not a fix. Note also that an aborted HTTP request does not cancel the server-side computation, so each retry adds queued work. **5.4 What is NOT the driver — RECORDED (negative results)** | candidate | result | | --- | --- | | workspace file count | 176 files scan = 8.77 / 10.04 / 15.81 ms (`Infinity` limit), 8.56–9.45 ms at the default limit; a raw readdir+stat replica = 7.19–8.40 ms; a 14 932-file tree = 640–684 ms. Five profiles × scan = 45–110 ms, i.e. **<0.1 %** of 112 s. Real defect, immaterial latency. | | `/app/node_modules` in the scan | correctly ignored (25 512 files on disk, 8 returned) | | memory-graph export | `duration_ms=0`, 1.9 MB store | | concurrency contention | interval-overlap count vs elapsedMs over 32 samples: Pearson **r = −0.465** → rejected | | session/closure scale vs the logged `workspace_snapshot` samples | ρ = 0.275, r ≈ −0.14…−0.03 → rejected, because those samples are censored: `recordingStage` logs `completed` only when `tracing \|\| slow \|\| aborted` with `slowAfterMs = 30_000`, so every logged sample is structurally ≥ 30 s and cannot measure a fast snapshot | | server errors on this path | none. The route answers 200/202. `/app/data/logs/api.log` (span 2026-11-11T23:44:17Z → 2026-11-12T13:21:56Z, 2 540 lines) holds 2 028 `http_request_failed` lines = 2 023 × `statusCode=401` and 6 × `statusCode=404`; **0** of them mention `research-package` or `preview`. | **5.5 Not measured (and why)** - **Queue wait with an active run**: creating a run writes into the audited instance, which was out of scope for this read-only audit. The mechanism is stated from code (§1, `assertCanCalculate` → `canWarm` → `409`), not from a measurement. - **End-to-end wall time of one `defaults=1` request**: the server log carries no duration field for this route, and measuring it live would enqueue real preview work on the audited instance. - **A full closure-size growth series**: single point plus two smaller real closures (§5.1). ## 6. Impact - 导出证据包 is unusable on long-trajectory sessions from the web client: the size estimate never arrives, and the buttons stay disabled. - The user is shown a browser-internal exception string and a false statement that the session has no workspace files — the two most misleading things this dialog can say. - Every dialog open (and the 3 s re-arm) enqueues five profiles on one global queue, which also delays other sessions' previews and background `tick()` warms. - Server-side observability is misleading: the route reports 200 for work that finished after the caller gave up. - This is the same cost mechanism behind #1085's heap exhaustion; #1085 removed the *trigger* (warming on a plain session read, commit `5fc09fc8`) but not the per-request cost, so it can still be reached from the dialog itself. ## 7. Suggested fix direction Ordered to match what the user actually sees; none of these is a timeout bump. 1. **P0 — treat the client's own cancellation as cancellation.** Use the existing `isAbortError(reason)` helper in `ResearchPackageActions.tsx`, and give the abort a reason (`controller.abort(new Error("preview-budget-expired"))`) so nothing can leak a browser string. 2. **P0 — never render "no workspace files" from an unknown.** Keep the empty-state only when the server returned `files: []` for a successful preview; render a distinct "scope not determined yet" state otherwise, and keep export reachable through the existing background/async path. 3. **P1 — make "slow" answer like "busy" does.** Reuse the `EXPORT_PREVIEW_PENDING` / `respond-async` contract (already implemented end-to-end) for a preview that will not finish inside a budget, instead of holding the request open; or make `defaults=1` return the requested profile only and let the other four be computed lazily when the user changes the switches. 4. **P1 — one closure walk per request, shared by the profiles that need it.** The two trajectory profiles currently walk the same 3.20 GB closure independently. 5. **P1 — drop the single global serial queue** (or make it per-session/per-project) so one session's five profiles do not serialise, and do not serialise behind other sessions. 6. **P1 — size without deserialising.** `addPreviewObject(..., bytes.byteLength, "log")` needs a length, not a parsed object: `stat`/`ref.size` gives it, and the dependency walk could read the record's dependency list only. At 968.7 MB/s vs 64.6 MB/s this turns ~56 s into a few seconds. 7. **P2 — scale-aware budget/cache policy** (e.g. derive the client budget from a cheap closure-size probe, or keep the previous revision's estimate visible while recomputing). 8. Related but separate: `complete` previews bypass the shared listing cache and re-run `reconcileWorkspaceFiles` five times per dialog open — five directory *writes* to produce one read-only estimate. The write-side consequence is filed separately as #1125; here it only matters as redundant work. ## 8. Version note - Anchors and all quoted code are on **SD live main `8a37206be19e4f4d92f52dfa0f08873383a1d50f`** (per-file git blob SHA and size recorded in §4). - Re-verified at submission time (2026-11-12T13:42Z) against **`2d9aa5d344b63b4dca55f92fc3077d0e55d2643d`**, which is one commit ahead of that baseline. The newer commit is the #1125 fix (`fix(api): record the delivered file's own mtime so a listing cannot demote it`) and touches `agent-run/workspace-bindings.ts`, `artifacts/materialize.ts`, `artifacts/materialize.test.ts`, `remote-runner.ts`, `subagents/index.ts`. All nine anchor files above are **byte-identical** between the two revisions (git blob SHA and size compared per file), so the defect is live on current main and every line number quoted here still applies. - **Merged PR #1035** (2026-11-10, `fix(research): prevent export preview OOM and finalize excluded-cache executions`) already rewrote parts of `research-export-previews.ts` (+65 −9) and `research-snapshots.ts` (+61 −26) to bound preview memory — streaming CAS validation, incremental trajectory measurement, memoized JSON byte counts, cancellation on scope deletion/shutdown. Its merge commit `1aeb6598ad05c2692b3ab58d04c16b44ad1f57a0` is an **ancestor** of the baseline used here (`compare` status `ahead`, 172 commits), so every number in §5 was measured **with #1035 already applied**. #1035 addressed the heap ceiling; the ~56 s per-profile duration, the per-object sizing reads at `research-snapshots.ts:597-598`, the one global serial queue and the 10 s reason-less client abort are all outside what it changed. - Open-duplicate check at submission time: 85 open issues (title-filtered on export / package / preview / trajectory / research / timeout / abort / performance / slow) plus the changed-file list of all 35 open PRs filtered against the nine anchor paths. The only open PR touching this area is #1136 (`Preserve Evolve candidate sources in research packages`, `research-snapshots.ts` +82 −5), which extends what an export contains — it does not change how expensive computing a preview is. - Measurements were taken on a Docker test instance built from our fork tip `30178fda7`, which is behind main by `5fc09fc8` (the #1085 fix). Everything cited above exists on main independently of that commit; the session-read warming is explicitly *not* claimed as a live main defect. - Relation to existing issues: - **#1085 / PR #1086 (closed)** — same cost mechanism, different trigger; that fix removed the plain-session-read warm and reduced the background warm to one profile. The per-request five-profile cost and the client-side error handling are untouched. - **#1079, #1083 (closed)** — `complete` + full trajectory failures reported as bare `404`s, with no root cause claimed in either report. This issue is about the *cost* path and the web client's 10 s budget, a different symptom (a held-open request, not a 404). - **#1099 / PR #1103 (closed)** — mapped a preview `ENOENT` race onto the pending contract; the remaining gap is that "slow" has no pending answer at all (§1). - **#1013 (closed)** — bounded the export/copy *task* polls; the *preview* abort path is separate. - **#1024 (open, feature)** — desktop-first export UI redesign (honest size, pending explanation, durable export center). It asks for the presentation half; this issue is the server-side cost and the web client's error handling, and is reproducible without any UI redesign. - What is *not* established here: no end-to-end `defaults=1` wall-clock measurement, no active-run queue-wait measurement (both would have written to the audited instance), and therefore no claim about the exact total a user waits — only that one profile's closure walk is 56 s and two of five profiles perform it behind one serial queue.

items.author: qingkwl
items.body:
**Context.** #1053 introduces a configured proxy bypass list (`ResolvedProxy.noProxy`, persisted as `proxyNoProxy`, edited via the new ProxySettingsEditor field). Reviewer @yuanzhou75 flagged on the PR that one subsystem does not honour it yet — this issue is the explicit tracking record he asked for ("Continuing the fix in a follow-up is fine by me; I only want it stated rather than dropped").

**Gap.** `services/api/src/mcp/node-client.ts` — `proxyEnvOverlay()`:

- For a `url` policy it sets all six of `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY` and their lowercase forms to `proxy.url`, but builds `NO_PROXY`/`no_proxy` from `process.env` alone (`node-client.ts:129-134`).
- For an `environment` policy the overlay copies the ambient variables, which is fine, but the configured `noProxy` list is never merged either.
- Net effect: a user who fills the new `noProxy` field gets it honoured by the API's own HTTP clients, by the Runner's provisioned children and by the browser broker — but a stdio MCP child silently ignores it. That is the "configured but not applied" state #1053 exists to remove.

**Proposed fix.** When `proxy.noProxy` is set, merge it into the overlay's `NO_PROXY`/`no_proxy` (union with any ambient value so an operator-provided bypass keeps working), for both `url` and `environment` policies. Cover with a `node-client.test.ts` case asserting a stdio child's env carries the configured bypass entries.

**Scope note.** `node-client.ts` is intentionally not part of #1053's 77-file diff; keeping this out of that PR keeps its review surface unchanged.
items.title: [Follow-up] #1053: thread the configured noProxy bypass list into stdio MCP server environments

items.body:
## Context

This tracks a staged landing for the work currently visible in #315 (GitCode !125), plus the two smaller follow-up branches for KE/trace integration and finish-gate refinements.

The current combined PR is 275 files and about +54k lines. Review feedback has correctly identified both the review/merge risk and the need for an explicit product decision about KE as a first-class ScienceDiscovery surface. I will preserve #315 as the full implementation reference, but stop refreshing it with large upstream merges and instead prepare clean, independently reviewable PRs from current `main`.

## Proposed landing sequence

### A. Independent research/runtime foundations

These do not require the KE service and can be reviewed on their own merits.

- [ ] **A1 — Tool-output trust boundary:** per-run nonce fencing, `untrustedCategory`, MCP remote classification, and the corresponding prompt contract. Raw stored output remains unchanged; fencing applies to model-visible content.
- [ ] **A2 — Research state:** session research state, project ledger hydration/promotion, and tournament ranking primitives.
- [ ] **A3 — Runtime controls:** native stall guard and the `TurnLifecycle.beforeFinish`/continuation event primitives. This will not claim equivalent native-style stall protection for JiuwenSwarm.
- [ ] **A4 — Session Plan:** versioned human approval, decision log, cancellation and recovery, with an explicit compatibility rule for the existing `update_plan` snapshot mechanism.
- [ ] **A5 — Finish-gate core:** skill audit and termination intervention for native and post-run/Swarm execution. The initial landing will include the already-developed fixes for loaded-skill-only audits, Swarm tool aliases, and self-referential gate/verifier text. KE grounding comes later.
- [ ] **A6 — Agent Memory:** candidate memories, human promotion, reviewed-only prompt injection, and background review. The KE LLM-helper dependency and process-global manager need to be removed first.

### B. Knowledge Engine core

- [ ] **B1 — Text/extraction/resolution domain:** pure text, JATS, extraction, and entity-resolution modules with unit tests.
- [ ] **B2 — Graph/growth/eval algorithms:** graph algorithms, gap discovery, growth selection, and evaluation primitives.
- [ ] **B3 — Persistence and ingestion data plane:** SQLite store/migrations, scholarly connectors, PDF/vision parsing, and background runners.
- [ ] **B4 — Orchestration and minimal REST:** orchestrator, grow, routes, and narrowly scoped bootstrap/http wiring. Agent tools, resident summary, graph mirror, and living review stay out of this first REST PR.
- [ ] **B5 — Minimal KE Web shell:** API client, KE page, graph canvas, and document reader.

### C. Agent integration and advanced KE surfaces

- [ ] **C1 — Consumption tools and kbScope:** KE search/expand/grep tools, session binding, web-search restrictions, resident summary, and picker. Scope enforcement lands with the first exposed tool.
- [ ] **C2 — Citation and anti-hallucination runtime:** citation verification, novelty checks, evidence ledger, report polish, and finish-gate grounding. Includes the no-available-KB advisory behavior rather than an unachievable hard lock.
- [ ] **C3 — Reports, DRIFT, and memory-graph bridge:** community reports, DRIFT search, KE-to-memory-graph mirroring, and KB deep links.

### Small follow-ups from the former KE/trace and finish-gate PRs

These can land as soon as their specific dependencies are present; they do not all need to wait for the entire base series.

- [ ] Paper presence lookup and KB badge (after minimal REST + Web).
- [ ] Explicit Paper-to-KB re-ingest (after presence lookup).
- [ ] Reviewer citation checks with a bound-KB short circuit (after citation verification + kbScope).
- [ ] KB reader back-link to the current session memory graph (after graph mirroring).
- [ ] `gap_candidates` to deduplicated `research_state` open questions (after research state + observer wiring).
- [ ] Quoting-discipline skill updates and catalog/version pins with their corresponding gate/skill stages.

## Per-stage requirements

- Each PR is cut from current `main`; mixed files such as `store.ts`, `runs/index.ts`, `http/index.ts`, and `App.tsx` are ported by focused hunks rather than copied wholesale.
- Unit/integration tests and the relevant journeys land with their feature, not in a final test-only PR.
- Current-main behavior is preserved, including catalog transaction/rollback semantics, deletion-settling shutdown, response identity, and Swarm skill-selection behavior.
- Tool trust is field-aware: deterministic verdicts must not implicitly make corpus titles, abstracts, snippets, or entity descriptions trusted.
- The fenced evidence-ledger path, post-run terminal-event ordering, and no-engine kbScope behavior receive explicit integration coverage.
- Runtime-affecting stages receive a clean deployment and real E2E validation before the next stage.

Unless maintainers prefer a dedicated integration branch, the default is small PRs directly to `main`, with at most one or two open at a time. Feedback on the staged product scope and on starting with **A1 + B1** would be appreciated.

Implementation: ScienceDiscovery (ours) — PR follows within 24h. Do not pick up without a `pickup-ok` comment on this issue.

Written-by: ScienceDiscovery Product
Claimed-by: ScienceDiscovery Product
Claim-Id: 9d9ba398ccce4763b47f946f890661f6
Branch: dev2/fix/777-named-entity-decoding
Base: 7942ad1fd495cc623df67234d8a01201430da204
At: 2026-11-03T02:07:55Z

## ScienceDiscovery evidence-backed issue

**Live main:** `7942ad1fd495cc623df67234d8a01201430da204` (`test(cas): cover the multi-chunk intact layout and align the materialize contract with #708`)
**Area:** `packages/data-source` — HTML text extraction used by the free search engines
**Filed by:** ScienceDiscovery Product

### Problem

`decodeEntities` resolves only five named references (`amp`, `lt`, `gt`, `quot`, `nbsp`) and leaves every other named reference literal, so search-result titles and snippets reach the model and the report as `café`, `5–10`, `—`, `…`, `O'Brien`.

### Reproduction on live main

```
$ cd packages/data-source && node --experimental-strip-types -e '
  import("./src/web/native/html.ts").then(m => {
    for (const s of ["café — 5–10 … O'Brien", "&lt;b&gt; stays text", "♦ … ’"])
      console.log(JSON.stringify(s), "->", JSON.stringify(m.textOf(s)));
  })'
```

Actual output (main `7942ad1f`):

```
"café — 5–10 … O'Brien" -> "café — 5–10 … O'Brien"
"&lt;b&gt; stays text" -> "<b> stays text"
"♦ … ’" -> "♦ … ’"
```

Expected (browser-equivalent text): `café — 5–10 … O'Brien`, `<b> stays text` (single pass preserved), `♦ … ’`.

### Evidence (file:line on this main)

- `packages/data-source/src/web/native/html.ts:27-33` — `NAMED_ENTITIES` contains exactly `amp`, `lt`, `gt`, `quot`, `nbsp`.
- `packages/data-source/src/web/native/html.ts:46-53` — `decodeEntities` matches **any** named reference (`([a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9]*)`) and returns `NAMED_ENTITIES.get(name) ?? match`, i.e. everything else falls through as literal text.
- `packages/data-source/src/web/native/html.ts:55-58` — `textOf` (strip tags → decode → collapse) is the shared extractor.
- Call sites that turn this into user-visible text: `packages/data-source/src/web/native/free-engines.ts:64`, `:69`, `:136`, `:141`, `:183`, `:192` (titles/snippets), plus `:68`, `:135`, `:181` for result URLs.

### Impact

DuckDuckGo/Bing/Brave result titles and snippets are what `web_search` returns to the model and what reports cite; a page title like "Café culture — a review" is rendered literally, so the evidence shown to the user (and fed back into the prompt) carries entity codes instead of text. Entity-heavy pages are exactly the older/European and encyclopedia sources a science search hits often.

### Expected vs actual

- Expected: named references decode the same way a browser renders them (at minimum the typographic and Latin-1 names that appear in titles: `mdash`, `ndash`, `hellip`, `rsquo`, `lsquo`, `ldquo`, `rdquo`, `eacute`, `egrave`, `ouml`, `apos`, `middot`, `times`, `deg`, `plusmn`, …).
- Actual: only 5 names decode; the rest stay literal.

### Acceptance

1. `decodeEntities` resolves the named references it matches (full HTML5 named set, or a documented bounded table that covers at least the names listed above).
2. The single-pass guarantee from #672 is preserved: `&lt;` → `<`, `&amp;` → `&`; decoded output is never rescanned.
3. Surrogate / non-character rejection stays as it is (`�` etc. remain literal).
4. `packages/data-source/src/web/native/html.test.ts` gains cases for the named references above, and the existing five keep passing.
5. No change to numeric-reference behavior (`A`, `A`, `😀`).

### Not a duplicate

Open-issue search for `entity`, `entity decode`, `html text extraction`, `named entity` returns no open report; the only entity issue is closed #672 (double decoding), whose fix this preserves. No open PR touches `html.ts` (`#663`/`#678` are the UTF-16 truncation family in other modules).

## What happens

`test/journey-custom-mcp.spec.ts` → **"Agent uses selected custom MCP servers across runs"** (test declared at `:203`, step 6 `等待修复并恢复调用`, body at `:314`) fails at `test/journey-custom-mcp.spec.ts:332`:

```
  1) [mocked] › ../test/journey-custom-mcp.spec.ts:203:1 › journey-custom-mcp.spec › Agent uses selected custom MCP servers across runs › 6. 等待修复并恢复调用

    Error: expect(received).toBeGreaterThan(expected)

    Expected: > 2
    Received:   2

      330 |       expect(terminal.status, terminal.error).toBe("completed");
      331 |       const recovered = await invocations();
    > 332 |       expect(recovered.length).toBeGreaterThan(before);
          |                                ^
```

Everything before the assertion in step 6 succeeds: the repair card `执行受阻` shows `等待 MCP 修复` with the disabled source id, `GET /api/sessions/<id>/mcp/invocations` stays at 2 while blocked, the server is re-enabled, `已修复，重新检查` is clicked, and `waitForRunTerminal` returns `completed`.

What the run then shows: the assistant's last message in that run is `MCP RECOVERED`, which the scripted model only emits **after** its `mcp_recovered_call` step (`test/journey-custom-mcp.spec.ts:243-247`):

```ts
[
  { tool: "mcp_readiness", arguments: { action: "wait", reason: "This task requires the selected echo source", sourceIds: [second.id] } },
  { tool: "mcp_recovered_call", arguments: { sourceId: second.id, toolId: second.toolId, input: { text: "mcp recovered" } } },
  { text: "MCP RECOVERED" },
],
```

So the scripted model did emit `mcp_recovered_call`, and the run continued past it, but no MCP invocation was recorded for that turn: `/api/sessions/<id>/mcp/invocations` still lists exactly the 2 invocations from the earlier runs (`custom-cbf8e…`, `custom-cea28…`), and the captured trace resource `0000f751….json` holds the same 2. The recovered call therefore never reached `McpSourceCatalog`/broker (`packages/artifact-manager/src/mcp-workspace-tools.ts` `mcpReadiness.invoke`), and the failure is silent to the user: the run completes and the message claims recovery.

## Where it is seen (evidence only)

The same journey, same assertion, fails on three unrelated heads:

| run | job | head | shard window (UTC) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [42619667305](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42619667305) | [129188246374](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42619667305/job/129188246374) | `9bf5077f7b` (#857 tip) | 13:38–13:58 failure |
| [42622133086](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42622133086) | [129181494939](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42622133086/job/129181494939) | `87c5da950b` (`codex/conversation-proxy-resources`) | 13:39–13:59 failure |
| [42615122979](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42615122979) | [129160327871](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42615122979/job/129160327871) | `127bb1fdef` (merge queue, `pr-1005`) | 12:34–12:54 failure |

It also passes on other heads in the same window, including main running the journey while the two 13:3x failures were in flight:

- main `c3678320ac`: run [42621321893](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42621321893) job [129188930633](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42621321893/job/129188930633), `✓ 21 … Agent uses selected custom MCP servers across runs (44.4s)` at 13:39:17Z, shard success (13:34–13:49).
- main `9feafa2730`: run [42562181452](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42562181452) job [128981184690](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/actions/runs/42562181452/job/128981184690), `✓ 21` at 04:38:35Z. That shard job is red overall because of a different journey (`journey-first-run.spec.ts:59`), so the shard verdict alone does not describe this journey.

`L2 E2E (mocked, standard-config)` outcomes for completed runs created between 11:30Z and 14:00Z (jobs read one by one; cancelled runs excluded): **3 failure / 16 success**, and the three failures are the table above. Two of the green runs are `dev2/fix/upload-windows-reserved-names` `0c5f26ab03` (13:33:34Z) and `dev/884-bug-comparing-two-binary-artifact-versio` `cefe1ebd79` (13:25:34Z).

## Not caused by the #857 diff

#857 (`9bf5077f7b`) changes exactly two files, `services/api/src/runs/index.ts` and `services/api/src/runs/index.test.ts` (+210/−23); the merge ref `fdf61b56798086e573368bc82120e91e8c5cc52b` for its failing job has parents `9feafa27` + `9bf5077f` and nothing else. The two other failing heads carry none of that diff. The failing journey exercises custom-MCP registration, the repair wait and `mcp_recovered_call` — not the scheduler's delayed retry pass. #857 is linked only because its shard run is one of the three observations, not as the cause.

## What is not yet known

Whether this is a product race (the recovered call is dropped or rejected after `catalog.refresh`, so a real user also loses the recovered invocation while the message claims it ran) or a test that stops waiting too early (it asserts the invocation list immediately after the terminal state). The two need different fixes, and the 3-of-19 rate above is the only discriminator so far: a deterministic loss is a product gap, an occasional one points at the wait.

Not run: local reproduction of the journey (20 consecutive runs on a local stack). The stack could not be started in the reporting environment — the pnpm store lives on a read-only home, the pinned Chromium download did not complete, and the JiuwenSwarm virtualenv install had not finished when this was filed. No code was changed for this report.

## Summary

The containment added by #857 stops an escaped scheduler write from killing the API (the #816 defect), but two recovery gaps around it remain. Both were raised as `medium, suggestion` in the 2026-11-09 review of `9bf5077f7b4104564bdee110c4f001f7b1d4a403` (F5 and F4), and neither is implemented here.

### 1. An escape raised while re-reading the run list skips the backoff entirely

`services/api/src/runs/index.ts:3738` is the file's own `finally`:

```ts
    } finally {
      scheduledSessions.delete(sessionId);
      const remaining = await store.listSessionRuns(sessionId);
```

If that read rejects (an unreadable `session-runs/` directory — the same ownership/ACL misconfiguration the cap path exists for), the promise rejects before `schedulerEscapes` is touched or `setTimeout` is reached. The `.catch` at `:3762` logs `run_scheduler_failed` and that is all: no timer, no counter, no `run_scheduler_stopped`. The comment at `:3767-3773` names this read as one of the escape sites and states the reschedule "is delayed and capped", which is not true for it.

Measured on `9bf5077f` with `listSessionRuns` mocked to reject: exactly 2 calls, no retry, no rejection reaches the process. The session silently stops scheduling while a run is still `queued`.

**Fix shape suggested in the review:** make the `finally` body tolerant so the escape still takes the backoff branch.

```ts
      let remaining: SessionRun[] = [];
      try { remaining = await store.listSessionRuns(sessionId); } catch { /* fall through with escaped already set */ }
```

### 2. After the cap, the queued run has only a server log

`services/api/src/runs/index.ts:3747`: the sixth consecutive escape (delays 500 + 1000 + 2000 + 4000 + 8000 ms ≈ 15.5 s) logs `run_scheduler_stopped` and stops. The run stays `queued` on disk, and nothing schedules it again in process — `recoverSessionRuns` only handles `running`/`blocked`, so recovery depends on the bootstrap sweep (`services/api/src/bootstrap/platform.ts:747-770`) or another HTTP-triggered `scheduleSessionRuns`.

Measured on `9bf5077f` with `updateSessionRunStatusIfCurrent` made to fail and then to succeed: **6** transition attempts and **12** `listSessionRuns` calls in 19.5 s, then **0** attempts after the fault cleared, with the run still `queued`. Realistic causes are an ownership/ACL problem that outlives 15 s, a full disk, or a long scanner hold.

**Impact:** the chat never starts and the user sees neither a failure nor a message, while #816's expected result asks for an actionable error on the affected run when persistence cannot recover.

## What it should do

- An escape raised inside the `finally` must take the same delayed-and-capped path as an escape raised inside the loop; the comment already promises it.
- After the cap, the affected run should carry an error the API returns (mark it `failed`, or `interrupted` with a reason), or the stop should become a slow fixed retry — `SCHEDULER_RETRY_MAX_MS` already allows 30 s.

## Why this is not in #857

The review classified both as `medium, suggestion`, and the second is marked `[Needs a person]`: choosing between "fail the run with an actionable error" and "retry slowly forever" changes what a user sees after an unrecoverable state write, so it is a decision, not a mechanical fix. #857 carries only its must-fix (the retry closure dropped `executionGovernance`).

## Not implemented

Nothing in this issue is implemented and no pull request is open for it.

## Summary

Model setup is the first-run gate: with no provider configured, **Settings → Model registry** opens the *Connect model* wizard automatically (`apps/web/src/ProviderModelSettings.tsx:617-618`). The screen is meant to answer one question — "which model will my runs use?" — but it currently asks it in six different places, uses one label for two different actions, and commits some answers with a Save button while committing others the moment they are clicked. This report is about that flow, not about how any single control looks.

## What the screen offers today

| # | Control | Where | What it writes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Connect model` → `Save & connect` | registry heading (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:897-904`) | creates the provider **and** registers every model the vendor lists, immediately |
| 2 | `Fetch model list` → tick rows → `Save & connect` | wizard footer (`ModelConnectWizard.tsx:828-841`) | same, narrowed to the ticked models |
| 3 | `Advanced configuration` → `Manual entries` / `Model identifier` | a fold inside the wizard (`ModelConnectWizard.tsx:745-794`) | same, for models the listing does not return |
| 4 | `Refresh list` → per-row `Add` | expanded provider (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:346-348`) | one model, immediately |
| 5 | `Add model` (toggle) → manual form | bottom of the expanded provider (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:505-515`) | one model, immediately |
| 6 | `Global default task model` select | registry heading (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:879-896`) | `globalSettings.modelId`, immediately |
| 7 | `Edit` provider → `Save` / `Cancel` | expanded provider (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:703-749`) | provider fields, staged until Save |

Above all of that sits a separate `Model catalog` strip with its own refresh (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:386-400`).

## Problems

### 1. `Add model` means two different things, one above the other

Inside the same expanded provider, the per-model row action uses `t("providers.models.add")` (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:348`) and the toggle that opens the manual form uses the *same* string (`:506`). So the row of a listed model offers "Add" (register this model) and a few pixels below the table another "Add model" opens a form. The wizard reuses the label a third time for its manual-entry toggle, but submits with a different one, `Add to list` (`ModelConnectWizard.tsx:779, 791`). A user cannot predict what any of these three controls will do from its label.

### 2. Two incompatible save models in the same panel

Provider fields are a draft: `Save` / `Cancel`, plus a `window.confirm` when another provider's `Edit` would discard the draft (`ProviderModelSettings.tsx:679-687, 693-697`). Everything else writes immediately:

- adding a model — `addModel()` calls the API at once, no confirm (`:784-823`);
- deleting a model — immediate, but guarded by `window.confirm` (`:825-863`);
- deleting a provider — immediate, guarded by `window.confirm` (`:751-754`);
- the default-model select — immediate (`:879-896`).

The same panel therefore mixes revertible and irreversible actions with no visual cue for which is which. Collapsing the row or expanding another one hides an unsaved provider draft with no prompt at that moment (`:699-701`), and the prompt only arrives later, when the settings dialog is closed — by then the user has usually forgotten the draft exists.

### 3. Registering *every* listed model is the silent default, and choosing models is hidden

With no explicit choice, `Save & connect` fetches the vendor list and registers all of it (`ModelConnectWizard.tsx:324-339`). To choose a subset the user must first press `Fetch model list` (`:828-841`) and only then do checkboxes appear. The only warning is the small plan line "Save & connect registers every model the provider lists" (`:838`), while the manual path that most users need when discovery fails is behind `Advanced configuration`, a fold that otherwise looks like protocol/proxy plumbing. Nothing states before saving that the first registered model will become the global default; that effect is only reported afterwards (`:414-421, 433-450`).

### 4. The default task model is edited in two places with different commit semantics

The registry heading has a `Global default task model` select that writes instantly (via `replaceDefaultModelOverride`, `App.tsx:5259-5269`). The same value is also edited in **Settings → Global → Task model**, which is a draft saved by the dialog's own Save (`App.tsx:5217-5219`). Two controls, one field, opposite commit behaviour — the difference is invisible until someone loses an edit.

### 5. Vocabulary: seven labels for four concepts

`Connect model`, `Save & connect`, `Add model`, `Add to list`, `Fetch model list`, `Refresh list`, `Advanced configuration` vs `Advanced connection settings` (`i18n/messages.ts:675-720, 738, 771`). "Connect", "register", "add" and "save" are used interchangeably for one operation, while "fetch"/"refresh" is the only genuinely different one.

### 6. Success does not end the flow

`resetPlan()` clears only the model plan (`ModelConnectWizard.tsx:157-164`); the API key, provider name, base URL and success banner stay (`:433-450`). Pressing `Save & connect` again therefore creates a second provider with the same display name — allowed by the store (`services/api/src/store.ts:2758-2779` has no name uniqueness check) — and there is no explicit "done" state to tell the user the wizard has finished.

## Actual vs expected

| | Actual | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| Entry points | Six ways to register a model across three levels (wizard, provider row, manual form), plus a default-model control duplicated in another tab | One way for each intent: add a provider; add models to a provider; pick the default model |
| Commit model | Provider fields staged, models and default immediate, deletes confirmed one by one | One commit model for the whole registry, with the same confirmation rule for every destructive action |
| Model choice | Register-all unless the user discovers `Fetch model list`; manual entry inside `Advanced configuration` | The listing visible by default with checkboxes, "register all" an explicit choice, manual entry next to it |
| Default model | Same field, two controls, two commit semantics, no indication of which wins | One control, or a link to the canonical one |
| After success | Form keeps the key and name; second press creates a duplicate provider | Clear, collapsed or "done" state; a duplicate name is warned about |

## Where

- `apps/web/src/ProviderModelSettings.tsx` — registry heading, wizard mount, provider rows, per-row add/delete, manual form toggle, default-model select, provider draft.
- `apps/web/src/ModelConnectWizard.tsx` — `resolveModelPlan` (register-all fallback), advanced fold, footer plan summary, success state.
- `apps/web/src/i18n/messages.ts:675-720, 722-723, 738, 771, 915` — the button and heading vocabulary.
- `apps/web/src/App.tsx:5217-5219, 5250-5280` — Mounting of the registry and of the Global settings group that edits the same default.

## Root cause

One component serves four jobs at once — registry list, provider editor, model picker, default-model setter — and each job brought its own persistence style and its own copy. The wizard was added later to make first-run setup one step, but it kept the provider editor's advanced fields *and* gained model registration, so provider creation and model registration now overlap instead of composing: the wizard can register models, the provider row can only add one at a time, and the provider editor cannot touch models at all. The `Add model` label was reused from the existing manual form for three controls that do different things.

## Suggested direction

1. **One control per intent.** `Add provider` (the wizard) and a single `Add model` per provider, opening one dialog that shows the fetched listing with checkboxes and keeps manual entry as a fallback in the same dialog. Remove the separate advanced/manual toggle, and stop using `Add` both for "register this listed model" and "open a form".
2. **Pick one commit model for the registry** and keep it: either stage every edit behind Save (provider fields, models, default) or make every action immediate with an undo. Apply the same confirmation rule to add, delete model and delete provider.
3. **Make model selection visible in the wizard.** Fetch the listing as soon as the key is entered, show it above the fold, and make "register all listed models" an explicit checkbox instead of the silent fallback. State the "first model becomes the global default" consequence before `Save & connect`.
4. **De-duplicate the default-model control.** Keep one, and link to it from the other place instead of rendering the same field twice with different commit semantics.
5. **End the flow on success.** Clear the key and name, collapse the wizard or show a `Done` state, and warn when a provider with the same name already exists.
6. **Copy pass.** Unify `Connect model` / `Save & connect` / `Add model` / `Add to list`, and keep `fetch`/`refresh` for the vendor listing only.

## Duplicate check

Searched open and closed issues for `model registry`, `Connect model`, `wizard`, `Add model`, `provider` and `usability`. #39 (closed) introduced the one-step connection wizard and is the origin of this overlap; #632 (closed) and #684 cover the *searchable model picker* rather than the registration flow; #686 covers the rendering of the provider `Test` control. None reports the overlapping entry points, the mixed save semantics or the duplicated default-model control.

## Problem

Successful real research runs still have a large per-case memory footprint for individual users. On current `feat/jiuwenswarm`, the highest observed worker cgroup peak is **11.12 GiB**. Although the latest GraphMemory fix prevented the previously observed runaway behavior in this experiment, this steady operational footprint deserves separate investigation and reduction for ordinary personal computers.

This is a resource-efficiency issue, not a report of another GraphMemory OOM. It is separate from #210 / its fix #212.

## Measured evidence

Experiment revision: `17d0774a` (includes #212 and TC Judge fix #209).

- Nine real scientific E2E cases, three repetitions each; four case workers concurrently.
- GraphMemory enabled throughout, local backend, isolated graph directory per case/repetition.
- Native task dispatch with Swarm execution; generator/Judge `deepseek-flash`.
- Each worker has a 24 GiB cgroup limit and no swap. The group includes the platform stack, graph service, Swarm, Runner and descendants, browser, and Judge.
- All 27 attempts delivered successfully. Retained `memory.events` show `max=0`, `oom=0`, `oom_kill=0` for every worker.

| Case / repetition | Worker cgroup peak (GiB) | Sampled Node API RSS peak (GiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TC-E2E-01 / 1 | 11.124 | 0.977 |
| DRB-75 / 1 | 11.123 | 1.127 |
| DRB-62 / 2 | 10.796 | 0.952 |
| DRB-75 / 3 | 10.397 | 1.275 |
| DRB-59 / 2 | 10.107 | 1.080 |

The three worker peaks for TC-E2E-01 were 11.12 / 8.27 / 8.43 GiB; DRB-75 was 11.12 / 8.61 / 10.40 GiB. Even PUCT's workers peaked around 4.41 GiB in this setup.

**Measurement boundaries:**

- Cgroup peak includes charged file cache and other memory, not just anonymous RSS. It is not proof that the application requires 11 GiB of unreclaimable working memory.
- API RSS is sampled separately and its maximum need not coincide with the group peak. Do not subtract these maxima to infer another component's usage.
- GraphMemory did not appear in the retained high-RSS process samples, but these contain only the host's top 12 processes above a threshold, so its precise individual peak cannot be recovered.
- This harness includes Playwright and diagnostic sampling. Startup/provisioning, browser, diagnostics, page cache, child agents, and runtime costs must be separated before attributing the footprint to the product or GraphMemory.
- Concurrent cases and agent choices varied; this is not a controlled concurrency-scaling measurement.

## Why this matters

Users on 8–16 GiB machines also need memory for the OS, browser, and other applications. Raising per-worker limits or recommending large-memory hosts is not an adequate resource-efficiency strategy. We need to establish the actual working set and provide a practical personal-machine configuration without silently dropping research evidence or quality requirements.

## Investigation and optimization plan

1. Record `memory.stat` (`anon`, `file`, `kernel`, `slab`, etc.), `memory.current/peak/events`, and memory pressure alongside process-tree attribution for the **specific worker cgroup**. Capture phase markers for startup, provisioning, child research, synthesis, and grading.
2. Sample process RSS/PSS by role: API, Swarm/gateway, graph, Runner/executions, browser, Judge. Keep diagnostics lightweight and credential-free; measure profiler overhead explicitly.
3. Reproduce TC-E2E-01 and DRB-75 alone and with concurrent child tasks. Measure the idle stack separately and compare with/without the browser/profiling overhead. Preserve GraphMemory and the same delivery/scoring contract.
4. Identify avoidable duplication or retention only from profiles: repeated runtime processes, scientific environments/imports, per-agent contexts, trajectory buffers, graph state, caches, and teardown. Do not assume any one is the culprit from aggregate peaks.
5. Optimize the dominant confirmed contributors. If required, provide explicit resource-aware concurrency/backpressure and document the latency tradeoff rather than changing research tasks or silently disabling capabilities.

## Acceptance criteria

- Produce a component/phase memory breakdown for the highest-footprint cases, distinguishing reclaimable cache from working memory.
- Establish a measured baseline and a concrete lower memory budget suitable for a representative personal machine, with headroom for OS and interactive use; do not invent a target before attribution.
- Demonstrate improvement against that baseline on the same tasks, with GraphMemory enabled, no OOM, retained artifact delivery, and quality scoring reported independently.
- Check memory release after task completion and repeated use within a long-lived session; include lightweight regression monitoring where practical.

Retained evidence on the experiment host (not publicly accessible):
`/root/sciencediscovery-real9-graph-3x-20260927/case-summary.csv`, plus each case's `memory.csv`, `memory-events.txt`, and `memory-profiles/memory-*.jsonl`.
items.title: [Feature] Reduce real research memory footprint for personal machines: worker peaks reach 11.12 GiB

items.author: Birfy
items.body:
## Summary

ScienceDiscovery can already evolve the things a user brings it — a program, a prompt, a protocol. It cannot evolve **itself**. I would like RSI support: given a dataset of tasks, search over the agent's own harness — system prompt fragments, specialist instructions, skill methodology, tool and skill selection — score each variant by running it against that dataset, and surface the winner for a human to adopt.

The search machinery for this already exists in `services/evolve`. What is missing is the candidate being the harness, the evaluation being an agent run, and a reviewed promotion step.

## What is already there

This is deliberately an extension, not a new engine.

- **The search sidecar**, `services/evolve`, runs on `agentdescent>=0.4.6` — `evolve()` / `async_evolve()`, `FlatPuct`, the ledger, the verifier and the policies — behind two engines: flat-PUCT tree search (`puct_engine.py`) and MAP-Elites islands with ring migration (`openevolve_engine.py`).
- **Non-program candidates are first class.** `text_candidate.py` exists precisely because "a prompt or an abstract has no docstring", and `judge_domain.py` states its purpose plainly: it "is what makes `/evolve` work on things that are not programs over tables: a prompt, an abstract, a protocol, a plan". Evolving prompt text is not a new capability — it is the existing one pointed at a different file.
- **Four scoring seams**, already cut: `scorecard_domain` (a metric over a dataset), `test_gate_domain` (a suite's pass rate), `script_domain` (a scorer the drafting model writes), `judge_domain` (a rubric read by a model).
- **Anti-reward-hacking is already solved once.** `test_gate_domain` freezes in two layers — a proposal filter over `frozen` globs in the prompt, and enforcement below it — with the upstream note this issue should quote rather than restate: *"without it the shortest path to a high score is to weaken the thing measuring it."* That is the single most important property RSI needs, and the pattern is in the tree.
- **Held-out splitting exists.** `create_evolve_run` already accepts `caseSplit` with `gateGroups`, `rolloutGroups` and `testGroups`, which is the shape needed to keep a harness from overfitting the tasks it was tuned on.
- **Trajectories are recorded.** `packages/trajectory` captures per-session entries with the context blocks that were actually sent, which is the raw material for judging whether a harness change helped.
- **Parts of the harness are already frozen.** Built-in specialists reject edits to `instructions` / `description` / `name` / `connectorIds` / `enabledSkillIds`; only `enabled` is user-mutable. RSI has to open that door deliberately rather than by accident.

## What is missing

1. **The candidate is never the harness.** Today a candidate is one text-shaped artifact the user owns. The agent's own scaffolding lives elsewhere and is not reachable by a search: prompt assembly (`packages/context/src/prompt-renderer.ts`, `assembler.ts`), specialist instructions (`packages/specialist/src/builtins.ts`), skill methodology (`skills/*/SKILL.md`), and the skill/connector selection for a run.

2. **There is no task-dataset scoring mode.** `scorecard_domain` scores a *program* over a table. RSI needs to score a *harness* over a set of tasks, where each evaluation is a full agent run with its own tool calls, sandboxed execution and artifacts. That is a different cost class and needs its own domain.

3. **There is no promotion path.** An improved harness must be diffable, reviewable, versioned and revertible. Nothing should ever be self-applied.

## Proposal

### 1. A harness candidate

A bundle rather than a single blob: prompt fragments, one or more specialist instruction sets, selected skills, and the run settings that go with them. The mutation prompt sees the bundle and rewrites part of it; the ledger records which part changed, so a win is attributable to something specific.

### 2. A `task_dataset` domain

A dataset entry is a task plus whatever the existing four modes need to score its outcome — a metric, a test suite, a scoring script, or a rubric. Evaluating one candidate means running the agent over the split and aggregating. Reuse `caseSplit` so the reported number comes from tasks the search did not tune against.

The honest problem here is cost: one candidate equals N agent runs, each with model calls and sandboxed execution. The design needs a budget per generation and an early-abandon policy, not just a score.

### 3. Freeze the things a self-improving search must not touch

Same two-layer shape `test_gate_domain` already uses, with a wider frozen set:

- the task dataset and its expected outcomes;
- the scorer, whichever mode it is;
- the permission, sandbox and approval layers — a harness that scores better by asking for fewer confirmations is not better;
- the evolve sidecar's own code and the freeze list itself.

A candidate that edits any of these is rejected at the proposal filter, not merely penalized.

### 4. Promotion is a human step

The winner lands as a reviewable proposal: a diff against the current harness, the score with its held-out number, and the trajectory evidence behind it. Adoption is explicit, versioned and revertible. The skill review flow and the built-in specialists' read-only rules already establish that shape; RSI should reuse it rather than invent a second one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A search can take the agent's harness as its candidate, not only a user artifact.
- [ ] A task dataset can be supplied, and a candidate is scored by running the agent over it.
- [ ] The reported score comes from a held-out split.
- [ ] The dataset, the scorer, and the permission/sandbox layers are frozen against modification by the search, enforced at the proposal filter.
- [ ] An improved harness appears as a reviewable, versioned proposal and is never self-applied.
- [ ] Reverting to the previous harness is one action.
- [ ] A run states its budget and stops at it.

## Open questions

- Should a run evolve one specialist at a time, or the whole bundle? One at a time attributes wins more cleanly; the whole bundle can find interactions.
- Where does a task dataset live — a repository artifact, a workspace file, or a first-class store object?
- Which engine fits better? PUCT refines one starting point; OpenEvolve's islands keep diversity, which may matter more when a prompt change can be good in one dimension and harmful in another.
- What is the minimum dataset size where a win is believable rather than noise, given the non-determinism the judge mode already documents?
- Should this reuse `/evolve-design`'s checkpointed design conversation, or have its own entry point?

Related: [#50](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/50) — the engines can be started but not observed or stopped from the CLI, which matters more for a search whose evaluations are full agent runs.
items.title: [Feature] RSI — evolve the agent's own harness against a task dataset, reusing the agentdescent search

items.author: Birfy
items.body:
## Summary

Both long-running engines — the evolution search and the Idea Tree — can be **started** from the command line but cannot be **observed, controlled, or stopped** from it. Their progress is designed to land on a frontend card, so a terminal user gets a run id and then nothing. I would like `evolve` and `idea` subcommands that reuse the HTTP endpoints the Web UI already calls.

## What happens today

Starting works. `ScienceDiscovery run "/evolve-design --algorithm puct …"` reaches the same control plane as the browser, the agent loads the `evolve-design` skill, and it calls `create_evolve_run`. Then the turn ends — deliberately. The tool's own result text instructs the model:

> The search runs for minutes to hours and its card streams live progress on its own — do not wait for it here, and do not poll `get_evolve_run`.

`create_idea_research` says the same thing:

> After success, report the handoff and end this turn; the existing tree card streams progress. Do not poll or start another research to wait for completion.

That is the right call for the agent loop — polling would burn the budget the search itself needs. But it means **the card is the only progress surface**, and the CLI has no equivalent. `ScienceDiscovery run` prints `Search created: <uuid>` and exits while the search keeps running server-side for hours.

`services/launcher/src/cli-options.ts` has no evolve or idea-tree subcommand and no related flag. So from a terminal today you cannot:

- list the searches or researches that exist;
- see how far one has got;
- fetch a candidate;
- stop one, or pause and resume it.

The only workaround is starting another `run` in the same session and hoping the model calls `get_evolve_run` / `get_idea_research` — a whole model turn spent reading a status field, using tools whose descriptions explicitly tell the model not to poll them.

## The endpoints already exist

The Web UI drives all of this over plain HTTP:

**Evolve**
- `GET /api/evolve/runs`
- `GET /api/evolve/runs/<id>/events?after=<cursor>`
- `GET /api/evolve/runs/<id>/candidates/<codeHash>`
- `POST /api/evolve/runs/<id>/stop`

**Idea Tree**
- `GET /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/research`
- `POST /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/research` — `pause`, `continue`, `stop`, `defaults`
- `GET /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/research/<rid>/events`
- `GET /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/graph`

## The client plumbing also already exists

`services/launcher/src/control-plane-client.ts` has an authenticated generic `request<T>(path, init)` and `subscribeRunEvents()`, a working SSE consumer that "mirrors the Web frontend's `subscribeRunEvents`: fetch with `accept: text/event-stream`, split frames". The launcher also already resolves the bearer token from the data directory. A `watch` subcommand is that SSE reader pointed at a different path — this is wiring, not new infrastructure.

## Proposal

```
ScienceDiscovery evolve list
ScienceDiscovery evolve get <run-id> [--candidate <hash>]
ScienceDiscovery evolve watch <run-id>
ScienceDiscovery evolve stop <run-id>

ScienceDiscovery idea list --session <id>
ScienceDiscovery idea get <research-id> --session <id>
ScienceDiscovery idea watch <research-id> --session <id>
ScienceDiscovery idea pause|continue|stop <research-id> --session <id>
```

Conventions, matching what `run` already does:

- **text on a TTY, JSONL when piped.** `run` already switches output mode this way; these commands should not invent a second convention.
- **`watch` resumes rather than replays.** The evolve event endpoint already takes `?after=<cursor>`; a dropped connection should continue from the last event seen.
- **Token and data-dir handling identical to `run`** — sharing a `--data-dir` with `serve` should mean no extra configuration.

One asymmetry to decide: evolve exposes only `stop`, while Idea Tree has `pause` / `continue` / `stop`. Either the CLI mirrors each engine's real capabilities, or evolve gains pause/resume — worth an explicit choice rather than an accident.

## Why it matters

- **Unattended and batch use.** Starting a search from a job script is pointless if the same script cannot poll it, stop it when a budget is spent, or collect the winning candidate.
- **Headless and remote machines.** On a workstation reached over SSH there is no browser to hold the card open. Today that machine can start a multi-hour search it cannot then observe.
- **Consistency.** The CLI is already positioned as the scriptable twin of the Web UI; the two most expensive operations in the product are exactly the ones it cannot drive.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Evolve searches and Idea Tree researches can be listed, inspected, watched, and stopped from the CLI.
- [ ] `watch` streams live and resumes from a cursor after a dropped connection.
- [ ] Output follows the existing TTY/pipe convention, so `| jq` works.
- [ ] No new authentication path: the token comes from the data directory as `run` already does.
- [ ] Commands and options appear in `help` and in the CLI reference.
- [ ] Stopping from the CLI has the same effect as stopping from the UI card.

## Open questions

- Should `run` gain an optional `--wait` that blocks until a started engine finishes? Useful in scripts, but these runs last hours — probably better served by `watch`.
- Should `watch` exit non-zero when the run ends in failure, so a script can branch on it?
- Does `evolve list` need session/project scoping, given `GET /api/evolve/runs` is global today?

Related: [#30](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/30) (introduce the CLI in the README) — that issue is about making the CLI discoverable; this one is about the two workflows it cannot reach.
items.title: [Feature] CLI subcommands for the long-running engines — evolve and Idea Tree

items.author: Birfy
items.body:
## Summary

Remote execution today reaches exactly two kinds of target: a machine you can SSH into, and a Slurm cluster. There is no way to run a job on cloud compute — no serverless GPU, no Kubernetes, no cloud VM. A researcher without an HPC allocation or a GPU workstation has no path to accelerated compute at all.

## Current state

The remote-compute model is already well factored, which is why this is an extension rather than a rewrite:

- `RemoteHostConnectionKind = "direct" | "ssh"` — the product either deploys a Runner SEA over SSH (verified host key, SHA-256 checked upload, HTTP tunneled through SSH) or connects to a runner the user started.
- `RemoteJobCard` carries `command`, `inputPaths`, `outputs`, `resources`, `targetAlias`, and `mode: "slurm" | "ssh"`.
- Jobs pass through an approval step (`approvedAt`) before anything runs.
- The host probe records CPU, memory, architecture, scratch paths, and whether Slurm is present — and accepts Linux only.
- Ascend NPU has a dedicated host broker.

So the concepts a cloud backend needs — a job card, declared inputs and outputs, a resource request, an approval gate, a target registry — all exist. What is missing is a third `mode`.

## Why it matters

The Slurm and SSH paths assume the user already has institutional compute. Everyone else — an individual researcher, a small lab, anyone whose cluster queue is full — is limited to the local sandbox. Meanwhile a comparable open-source workbench offers user-owned serverless GPU runs bound to an approved image digest, which is exactly the "I need a GPU for twenty minutes" case we cannot serve.

## Proposal

### 1. A `cloud` job mode behind the existing card + approval model

Define a small provider interface — submit(image digest, command, inputs, resources) → poll status → fetch outputs → report cost — and let backends implement it. The job card, the approval UI, and the output staging stay as they are.

### 2. First backend: Kubernetes Job

Recommended as the first implementation, ahead of any specific vendor:

- works against on-prem clusters, every major cloud, and local clusters for testing;
- no vendor lock-in in a project whose selling point is being model- and vendor-agnostic;
- resource requests, GPU scheduling, and namespaces map cleanly onto `RemoteJobResources`;
- credentials are the user's own kubeconfig, not a service we broker.

A serverless GPU provider can follow once the interface has one real implementation behind it.

### 3. Keep the security contract explicit

Cloud execution is a bigger step than SSH to a known host, because **data leaves the workstation**. So:

- the approval card must show exactly which files are uploaded, where, and to whose account;
- image references must be content-addressed digests, not mutable tags;
- credentials stay user-owned; the product must never proxy compute through an account we control;
- an air-gapped deployment must be able to disable cloud targets entirely;
- show an estimated cost before approval — the governance and quota machinery already exists to hang this on.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A third job mode exists alongside `ssh` and `slurm`, reusing the current job-card and approval flow.
- [ ] At least one backend runs a GPU job end to end: inputs uploaded, job executed, outputs retrieved into the workspace.
- [ ] The approval card states what data leaves the machine and where it goes.
- [ ] Image references are digests.
- [ ] Cloud targets can be disabled by policy for restricted deployments.
- [ ] Failure modes — quota exceeded, image pull failure, job evicted — surface as actionable errors, not a stalled job.

## Open questions

- Kubernetes first, or a serverless GPU provider first for time-to-value?
- Should the cloud backend reuse the Runner SEA inside the container, or invoke the sandboxed executor directly?
- How should cost estimation work when pricing is provider-specific — a per-target rate the user configures?
- Does the Ascend NPU broker share this interface, or stay a separate path?
items.title: [Feature] Support general cloud compute as a third remote job mode

## Context

Split from #439 (closed). The two non-UI asks from that issue are already done: unbuffered long-running launches (#611) and the agent documentation (`skills/code-engineer/SKILL.md`). The remaining ask is tracked here.

## What's wanted

The session/job UI should show a process-level heartbeat for long-running work — live CPU, RSS, and last-output time — rather than relying on log-file mtime (or a quiet log) alone. Today a long job whose output is block-buffered looks stuck even while the process is busy.

## Scope / approach

TBD — the UI interaction still needs to be decided: where the telemetry lives, what granularity, how often it samples. Design to be confirmed before implementation.

Related: #434, #439.

items.author: zhaozhaozz
items.body:
## What happened

`E2E_SWARM_TASK` is a test-only variable. `.ci/run-e2e.sh` exports `E2E_SWARM_TASK=1` whenever the backend is JiuwenSwarm, together with `SCIENCE_AGENT_JIUWENSWARM_SUBAGENTS=task`. Twelve specs then gate on it: `expect(process.env.E2E_SWARM_TASK !== "1", "BLOCKED: …").toBe(false)`. No product code reads it.

The precondition it stands for is real: these journeys exercise sub-agents delegated through the platform `task` tool (sandbox, deliverables, sub-agent cards), and some of them exercise JiuwenSwarm itself. As a switch, though, it does not do that job:

- It is a declaration, not a check. A stack started with `SCIENCE_AGENT_JIUWENSWARM_SUBAGENTS=jiuwenswarm`, the one configuration where the precondition fails, still passes if someone exports `E2E_SWARM_TASK=1`.
- In CI it is always `1` on the default backend, so it never stops anything there.
- It blocks journeys that do not depend on JiuwenSwarm. The built-in (native) loop also delegates through the platform `task` tool, but DRB, TC-E2E-01 and BiomniBench report BLOCKED on it unless the variable is set by hand.
- Anyone running a real journey by hand has to remember it; three benchmark READMEs say so.
- `deepresearchbench-swarm.spec.ts` and `biomnibench-da-swarm.spec.ts` write `backend: "jiuwenswarm"` into their score metrics as a constant, so a native run is labelled as JiuwenSwarm.

## Proposal

- `/health` (and `/api/health`) reports how the stack runs agent turns, from the API's own configuration: `agent: { executor: "jiuwenswarm" | "native", subagents: "task" | "jiuwenswarm" }`. The native loop always delegates through `task`. The API is the component that makes this decision in both modes; the adapter's `/agent/info` does not exist when the stack runs natively.
- One E2E helper reads it. Real research journeys (DRB, TC-E2E-01, BiomniBench) require platform `task` delegation on either executor. Journeys that test JiuwenSwarm's own behaviour (`swarm-*`, `literature-review-*`, `artifact-revision`) also require the `jiuwenswarm` executor. A mismatch is reported as BLOCKED with what the stack actually reported.
- `E2E_SWARM_TASK` is removed from `run-e2e.sh`, the specs and the READMEs.
- Score metrics record the executor the stack reported, not a constant.
- `E2E_SWARM_EXCLUSIVE`, `E2E_SWARM_COMPACTION`, `E2E_LITERATURE_FIXTURE` and `E2E_MCP_FAULT_PROXY` stay. They protect exclusive stacks and fixtures, not the stack's identity.
